# “Take Nothing on Its Look”: Revealing Users’ Expectations and Experiences in Social Human–Robot Interaction

Authors: Jessica Lindblom, Julia Rosén, Maurice Lamb, Erik Billing Authors Info & Claims

ACM Transactions on Human-Robot Interaction, Volume 15, Issue 2

Published: 22 December 2025 Publication History

Contents

### Abstract

The use of social robots in many sectors of society is predicted to progressively increase. Therefore, exploring how expectations play a role in and change users’ experiences when interacting with these robots over time is necessary. From an interpretative and insight-driven approach, our aim was to explore how humans experience in-person interactions with the social robot Pepper, which was equipped with the OpenAI GPT-3 language model. Qualitative data from 62 video recordings of the interactions with Pepper and post-test interviews were collected from 31 participants. An experiential reflexive thematic analysis was applied. The main findings include various levels of interaction quality, different interaction strategies, and elements influencing the users’ expectations and experiences, which were synthesized into a coherent framework. It appears that the participants adapted their interaction strategies based on their expectations and the perceived capability of the robot, which influenced their experiences. This reveals that positive user experience is not solely determined by interaction quality, showing the interplay among these aspects when interacting with a social robot. To conclude, our findings underscore the intricate nature of the role of user expectations and experiences in social human–robot interaction. The work adds complementary qualitative approaches to the Human–Robot Interaction community to provide additional insights on interacting with social robots.

## 1 Introduction

The ability to participate in various types of social interaction and cognition is a crucial building block for the ability to be situated and embedded in human culture [39, 40, 44, 90]. In Social Human–Robot Interaction (sHRI), social robots can be autonomous or semi-autonomous artifacts intentionally created to interact and communicate with humans by adhering to expected behavioral norms. Anthropomorphic or zoomorphic features typically characterize them and are specifically designed to engage in social interactions with people [1, 13, 25, 36, 68]. Accordingly, sHRI spurs the ongoing development of emerging and new interaction paradigms for how humans should interact, communicate, and relate to these socially interactive artifacts [14, 15, 19, 20, 25, 74]. It is still an open question how humans should understand and interact with social robots since this challenge spans several dimensions [cf. 18, 88, 90]. The role and relevance of users’ expectations and experiences of social robots are central dimensions of these challenges and are the main topic of this article.

The study of users’ expectations towards social robots is still an emerging area within the interdisciplinary sHRI field. There is a need to narrow the knowledge gap about how expectations influence users’ experiences of sHRI. Social robots are likely to be increasingly important in our everyday lives. Their degree of participation in everyday activities in society is envisioned to becoming more sophisticated, resulting in greater expectations of these interactive technologies from their intended users [3– 6, 20, 21, 29, 31, 37, 40– 43, 48, 67]. Given that social robots are both digital artifacts and exhibit the appearance of agency as found in biological creatures [90], they are often either positively experienced as fascinating or negatively experienced as frightening [1, 56]. Social robots, therefore, still blur the distinction between a thing and an agent [1], resulting in several challenges for users regarding what to expect when interacting with social robots. Although there is an increase in sHRI studies that focus on User Experiences (UXs) of social robots, various ways of conceptualizing UXs in sHRI exist [88]. To complicate the issue further, most people, both potential users and participants in research, have either no first-hand experience or limited experience of interacting with social robots. As such, exposure to social robots is predominantly from movies and the media, which may result in misleading and inaccurate expectations and experiences of social robots [59, 64, 67, 71, 75]. Clarke and Fischer [18] pointed out that attributing human-like capabilities to socially interactive artifacts like social robots is not the same as engaging in Human–Human Interaction (HHI). When humans initially encounter a particular social robot first-hand, they often have little knowledge of its capabilities, particularly its social interaction skills. This uncertainty presents various challenges, such as determining which actions the robot can recognize and respond to and how interactions should be performed to ensure an effective response by the robot [81]. Therefore, the types and role of expectations in sHRI cannot be directly inferred from research on expectations in HHI.

In social psychology and cognitive science, expectations are well acknowledged as an underlying aspect of social interactions in shaping our beliefs about the future [60, 65]. Although there have been some attempts at the intersection of UXs and expectations in the Human–Robot Interaction (HRI) community (e.g., [35, 45, 52, 64, 86]), expectations are rarely studied explicitly. However, HRI studies often touch on expectations in implicit ways, indicating that user expectations can significantly influence people’s experiences with social robots [e.g., 8, 21, 26, 31– 33, 35, 38, 45, 47, 49, 52, 54, 55, 62, 67, 71, 76].

In Human–Computer Interaction (HCI) and UX, it is well acknowledged that users’ expectations when interacting with digital systems, products, or services are a core aspect before, during, and after interaction [29, 73, 78]. In sHRI, the role and relevance of expectations have yet to be systematically investigated and analyzed from a first-hand perspective. Hence, as expectations change over time, including during interactions, it is crucial to understand what elements support these changes and how previous experiences influence the present interaction quality when interacting with social robots. More human-like robots seem to engage humans to interact with them, given that their human-like appearance and behavior tend to generate high expectations of their social interaction capabilities [81]. Individuals who encounter a social robot for the first time or have limited experience interacting with them are especially revealing to study, since they cannot rely on prior knowledge of the social robot’s social interaction abilities. They therefore have to rely on their expectations and what they discover about those skills. As pointed out by Tuncer et al. [81], there is a need for a shift in sHRI studies, which changes the focus from merely perceptions of social robots, predominantly studied by questionnaires, to qualitative insights from analysis of individuals’ expectations and experiences when interacting first-hand with a social robot over time [81].

The purpose of this article is to explore and provide insights into how humans, as users of robots, experience first-hand interactions with social robots. It also aims to deepen the understanding of what elements influence their expectations over time. Qualitative data on human expectations of social robots were collected through video recordings and post-test interviews from an experimental setup, investigating first-hand experiences interacting with the social robot Pepper [2], equipped with a customized dialogue system operated by the OpenAI GPT-3 language model. The study was exploratory and interpretative [82], which means that the first-hand experience was based on an open scenario in which limited guidance was provided to the participants regarding how they should interact with the social robot, beyond the instruction that they should try to get to know the social robot designed for home environments, mainly as a social companion. Their task in this scenario was to interact freely with the robot and ask questions. Participants were encouraged to explore ways they found natural or interesting, trying different questions to explore how the robot would respond, while getting to know the robot. It should be mentioned that the quantitative results from this study have been reported in Rosén et al. [72], revealing a relatively strong influence on user expectations. While many participants did change expectations over time when interacting with the social robot, previous experiences with robots were shown to be a major factor in how participants experienced the robot. These results indicate that users’ feelings towards robots, assessed using common measures such as the Negative Attitudes towards Robots Scale (NARS) [57] and the Robot Anxiety Scale (RAS) [58], are to a large extent influenced by factors happening before the interactions with the social robot take place. The results of the quantitative study also show that the attitudes of the users, assessed using NARS, were more stable over time than the altered behavior assessed using RAS.

This article aims to provide a deeper understanding and additional insights into how individuals’ expectations influenced the first-hand sHRI and how humans experienced these situations over time. Most participants had limited or no first-hand experience interacting with social robots. The following five objectives address the aim:

exploring various levels of interaction quality,

exploring what kinds of interaction strategies the participants used,

exploring how participants’ explicit expectations changed over time,

exploring the core elements of the sHRI and the social robot that influenced the participants’ expectations and experiences, and

exploring participants’ experiences and generalizing them into UX dimensions.

This article provides insightful qualitative findings from an experiential reflective thematic analysis [11, 12, 17] of the qualitative data collected during the open scenario. As noted by Veling and McGinn [82], qualitative studies that are exploratory and interpretative offer powerful tools, although lacking the precision of hypothesis-driven experiments. Thematic and qualitative approaches can therefore grasp human perspectives and aspects of interactions to reveal new explanations and understandings [10– 12, 82].

The remainder of the article is organized as follows. Section 2 provides a background to expectations and UX from a more theoretical perspective, previous research on expectations in HRI and sHRI, and the social robot expectation gap. The methodology is motivated and described in Section 3, including the participants, the material and the procedure, and the data analysis.
